missing_buckets.title: Demand-Side Emergency Management: Can fuel demand be suppressed or deferred to extend product inventory runway while supply is constrained?
missing_buckets.rationale: The entire decomposition focuses on supply-side interventions (sourcing, run-rates, finance, diplomacy). No bucket explicitly addresses demand-side levers — the other half of the supply-demand balance. At 40% throughput across 6 refineries, even successful crude procurement may produce insufficient product volume to meet all obligations. Temporary demand suppression (rationing, price signals, sectoral priority) could extend the product runway by days or weeks, buying time for supply-side solutions. This bucket is entirely absent and is not a sub-question within any existing section.

questions.question: What emergency demand rationing measures — including odd-even dispensing at fuel stations, priority-only allocation for essential services (military, hospitals, agriculture, public transport), and suspension of non-essential aviation routes — could MoPNG and state governments implement within 48 hours to reduce effective HSD and MS demand by 15–25%, and what is the estimated product inventory runway extension (in days) that each measure would provide at each refinery's hinterland?

Are there large industrial HSD consumers (captive power generators, mining, construction) in the hinterlands of the at-risk refineries that could be directed to switch to alternative fuels (natural gas, coal) or reduce operations during the crisis period under emergency MoPNG directives — and what volume of HSD demand reduction (in kbpd equivalent) could realistically be achieved through industrial demand management within 7 days?

Can the Ministry of Civil Aviation temporarily reduce domestic flight frequencies or suspend non-trunk routes to cut ATF demand, freeing refinery throughput capacity for LPG and HSD production — and what is the estimated ATF demand reduction from a 20% domestic capacity cut, and does it create sufficient product yield rebalancing headroom at the constrained refineries?

What is the product inventory position in the OMC depot and retail network (not just at-refinery stocks as in 1.5) for each hinterland — specifically, how many days of demand do the combined pipeline, depot, and retail-level inventories cover even if refinery output drops to zero today, and which hinterlands have the longest and shortest total system inventory buffers?

Has MoPNG or PPAC modeled a product demand triage framework that explicitly prioritizes (1) LPG for domestic cooking, (2) HSD for agriculture and essential transport, (3) MS for emergency services, and (4) ATF for designated essential air routes — and can this framework be operationalized as a formal supply allocation directive to OMCs and state oil companies within 24 hours, enabling controlled supply rationing rather than a first-come-first-served depletion?

missing_buckets.title: Legal and Contractual Risk Management: What is the exposure from existing contracts, and what legal instruments protect refineries during the crisis?
missing_buckets.rationale: The decomposition addresses financial solvency, regulatory waivers, and sanctions law in passing across multiple sections, but there is no dedicated bucket for the contractual and legal risk dimension: force majeure declarations on crude purchase contracts, product supply agreement defaults, offtake contract violations, insurance claim activation, directors' liability for continued negative-GRM operations, and the legal instruments available to MoPNG to direct PSU refiners to operate against their boards' fiduciary interests. These legal questions are distinct from the financial and stakeholder buckets and require dedicated treatment.

questions.question: For each of the 6 refineries, do their existing crude purchase contracts with Saudi Aramco, ADNOC, SOMO, and KPC contain force majeure provisions that the Indian refiner can invoke in the event of inability to pay due to the financial crisis — and if invoked, do these clauses suspend payment obligations without triggering contract termination or supply suspension, and has MoPNG's legal counsel identified which contracts offer the most protective FM language?

Do the boards of HPCL, BPCL, CPCL, IOCL, and NRL have a legal fiduciary obligation to halt operations if continued refining at $156/bbl crude generates sustained negative GRM — and does a written MoPNG ministerial directive instructing continued operations provide legal protection to individual directors against shareholder or regulatory action for operating at a loss, or does this require a formal Presidential Directive under the Companies Act?

What product supply contracts (with state governments, aviation companies, defense establishments, fertilizer plants) do the 6 refineries have that would be defaulted upon if throughput falls below minimum supply obligations — and what is the aggregate contractual liability (penalty clauses, replacement cost obligations) from such defaults, and has MoPNG assessed whether declaring a national energy emergency would provide statutory protection from these claims?

Have the refinery legal teams identified all insurance policies (property, business interruption, cargo, war-risk) that may be triggered by the current crisis — specifically, does the Hormuz mining event qualify as a covered peril under business interruption insurance for refineries that face crude shortfall, and have claims been filed or notices of circumstance been issued to insurers within the required notification windows?

Under the Essential Commodities Act or the Petroleum and Natural Gas Regulatory Board Act, what emergency powers does the Government of India have to compulsorily direct private refiners (Reliance, Nayara) to supply product to deficit regions, share crude with PSU refiners, or limit product exports — and has MoPNG assessed the legal basis and political feasibility of exercising these powers within the 72-hour window?

duplicate_flags.reason: 2.3 asks about SPR drawdown authorization timeline within 72 hours. 6.7 mentions SPR expansion as a long-term restructuring decision. While time horizons differ (immediate vs. 60-day strategic), the SPR drawdown activation mechanism is addressed in 2.3 and the 6.7 reference to SPR is subordinate/implied — not a true duplicate but worth confirming 6.7 does not re-ask the 72-hour SPR question.

1.9 asks for GRM at $156/bbl and the crude price at which GRM turns negative per refinery. 4.1 asks for per-day under-recovery at $156/bbl and the cumulative days until working capital exhaustion. Both require computing GRM and under-recovery at the same crude price — they are asking for the same calculation from slightly different angles (financial trigger price vs. cash-flow runway). These should be consolidated or one should explicitly reference the output of the other to avoid duplicative financial modeling effort.

3.5 asks whether deficit MS/HSD output can be covered by emergency product imports within 15 days. 6.3 asks whether PPAC has a time-phased product demand priority matrix updated for MRPL shutdown. Both implicitly require a product deficit volume calculation — the supply gap number computed in 3.5 is prerequisite to the allocation in 6.3. These are not strict duplicates but share a common analytical foundation that should be explicitly linked to avoid redundant computation.

2.9 asks about war-risk insurance premiums, P&I club suspensions, and GIC Re government-backed war-risk cover as a barrier to crude procurement. 4.9 asks about war-risk insurance premium per voyage per origin-destination pair and aggregate additional insurance cost per barrel, also referencing GIC Re reinsurance. These two questions ask substantially the same question from sourcing and financial angles respectively — the war-risk cost and GIC Re backstop question is effectively duplicated and should be merged.

5.4 asks about Indian banks' secondary sanctions exposure from Russian crude LCs and contingency payment mechanisms. 7.4 asks whether RBI has issued or should issue a directive to Indian banks to maintain PSU refinery LC facilities without additional collateral. Both require RBI engagement on LC support for crude purchases — 5.4 focuses on Russian crude specifically and 7.4 on all crude LCs, but the RBI directive question and the bank LC stress question are substantially overlapping and the answers inform each other.
